newsitem.title: UK: EMERGING MARKET OUTLOOK - BULGARIA, RUSSIA IN VIEW.
newsitem.headline: EMERGING MARKET OUTLOOK - BULGARIA, RUSSIA IN VIEW.

text.p: Eastern Europe will dominate the emerging market scene this week with a knife-edge decision from Bulgaria and details of Russia's forthcoming Eurobond spelling a heady week for investors.

BULGARIA will be keeping investors on the edge of their seats once again. The International Monetary Fund last week said the country had a choice between implementing a currency board or sustaining high interest rates and expects a decision this week.
"It's make or break in Bulgaria," said one east European economist. "If the IMF pulls the plug, Bulgaria will find it difficult not to default on its debt."
He said the idea of a currency board was a good provided it was properly implemented and had the necessary backing, but he acknowledged it was provoking considerable dissent internally.
RUSSIA's roadshow rolls across Europe, Asia and the United States starting on November 11, with Finance Minister Alexander Livshits attending the Frankfurt and London presentations.
Investor speculation on the price of the landmark bond, Russia's first, has veered widely with some mooting a spread around 350 basis points over Treasuries.

"That looks pretty speculative at the moment," said Peter West, emerging market economist a West Merchant Bank. But he added there were no other benchmark deals in the market against which this issue could easily be priced.

"Now that (Russian President) Boris Yeltsin seems to be making a rapid recovery, it's probably going to come out pretty tight," he said, adding that a level below 400 basis points was not out of the question.
Douglas Helfer, senior analyst for Russia at Foreign & Colonial, said while the eurobond issue was not particularly large it was of considerable psychological importance to Russia.
The International Monetary Fund is also due to return to the country and investors will be hoping for word on the release of a delayed loan tranche.
A FOMC meeting in the United States next week was less of a market factor, since few players seriously expect any move.
"It's really a non-event," the economist said.

In Latin America, BRAZIL heads into the second round municipal elections on November 15, and investors will be watching keenly for signs of sentiment on whether President Fernando Henrique Cardoso should be allowed to stand for a second term.

More immediate will be the release of import data for October to match the 4.2 billion October export figures. Investors have been particularly worried after September numbers came in worse than expected.
But strong capital inflows, including direct foreign investment, will allow Brazil to finance a bigger trade deficit, one Latin American economist said.
ECUADOR is due to announce its long awaited economic programme on November 16.

"There is a lot of speculation on whether they will go for a fixed exchange rate or a currency board plan to get inflation down," said West Merchant Bank's Peter West. "They will be looking for an orthodox plan to bring down the fiscal deficit."
That deficit is currently running at about 3.0 percent of GDP, which is much higher than official projections.
In the Middle East, EGYPT hosts a two-day economic summit starting on Tuesday aimed at integrating ISRAEL into the regional economy.

And in Asia, Thailand heads into national elections on Sunday, November 17. Investors hope this will bring to an end some of the political turbulence that has hit its equity markets severely this year.
The IFC composite index of emerging market equities, denominated in dollars IFC/IPRD, was up 0.7 percent week on week at 292.17 on Friday.
Latin America was up 0.9 percent at 528.29, Asia was up 1.7 percent at 250.78, and Europe, Middle East and Africa was quoted down 1.9 percent 134.31. --London Newsroom +44 171 542 2734
